token.def: The unit a language model reads and writes: a whole word, a piece of a word, a punctuation mark or a byte, as its tokenizer splits the text. Cost, speed and context limits are all counted in tokens.

bpe.def: A way to learn a subword vocabulary: start from characters or bytes and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, until the vocabulary reaches its target size.

byte-level-bpe.def: BPE that starts from the 256 byte values instead of characters, so any text, in any script or with emoji, can be encoded without an unknown token.

vocabulary.def: The fixed set of tokens a model knows, each with an id. Modern LLMs use roughly 32,000 to 260,000 tokens.

token-tax.def: The extra tokens a language needs, compared with English, to say the same thing on a given tokenizer. It raises cost and latency and leaves less room in the context window.

attention.def: The operation that lets each token gather information from other tokens: a weighted average of the other tokens' value vectors, weighted by how well the token's query matches each key.

qkv.def: Three vectors computed from each token by learned matrices. The query is what a token looks for, the key is what it offers to be matched on, and the value is what it passes on when matched.

cross-attention.def: Attention in which the queries come from one sequence (the decoder's) and the keys and values from another (the encoder's output).

multi-head-attention.def: Several attentions run in parallel on narrower projections of the same vectors, their outputs concatenated and mixed by one more matrix, so different heads can track different relations.

causal-mask.def: A mask that stops a token attending to later tokens: their scores are set to minus infinity before softmax, so their weights are exactly zero.

positional-encoding.def: Information about each token's position added to a transformer, which would otherwise treat its input as an unordered set.

rope.def: A positional encoding that rotates pairs of query and key dimensions by angles proportional to the position, so the attention score depends only on the distance between two tokens.

residual-stream.def: The vector per token that runs through a transformer. Each sub-layer adds its output to it (a residual connection) instead of replacing it.

rmsnorm.def: Normalisation that divides a vector by its root mean square and multiplies by a learned gain. Pre-norm models apply it before each sub-layer.

ffn.def: The part of a transformer block applied to each position on its own: widen the vector, apply a non-linearity, project back. It holds about two-thirds of a dense model's parameters.

swiglu.def: A feed-forward layer with a gate: one matrix decides how much of a second matrix's output to let through, and a third matrix projects the result back. Used by most current LLMs.

gqa.def: Attention in which groups of query heads share one key head and one value head, which shrinks the KV cache with little loss in quality.

encoder-only.def: A transformer whose tokens all see each other (bidirectional attention), trained to fill in masked tokens. Used for classification, embeddings and rerankers.

decoder-only.def: A transformer with a causal mask, trained to predict the next token. The architecture of GPT-style LLMs.

encoder-decoder.def: A transformer whose bidirectional encoder reads the input and whose causal decoder writes the output, attending to the encoder through cross-attention. Used for translation and speech recognition.

logits.def: The raw, unbounded scores a model outputs, one per vocabulary token, before softmax turns them into probabilities.

softmax.def: The function that turns a vector of scores into probabilities: exponentiate each score and divide by the sum. Adding the same constant to every score changes nothing.

autoregressive.def: Generating one token at a time, each appended to the input before the next is predicted.

prefill-decode.def: The two phases of generation: prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass; decode then produces one token per forward pass.

cross-entropy.def: The training loss of a language model: the average of −log p of the token that actually came next. Lower is better; ln of the vocabulary size is what a uniform guess scores.

kv-cache.def: The keys and values of earlier tokens, kept in memory during generation so each new token only computes its own. It grows linearly with context and is often the memory limit in serving.

temperature.def: A decoding setting that divides logits before softmax: below 1 sharpens the distribution, above 1 flattens it, and towards 0 it approaches greedy decoding.

greedy-decoding.def: Always choosing the most probable next token.

top-k.def: Sampling only from the k most probable tokens, after renormalising their probabilities.

top-p.def: Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p, after renormalising.

moe.def: A model in which each feed-forward layer is replaced by many expert networks and a router that sends each token to a few of them, so most parameters are stored but not used for any one token.

router.def: The small learned layer in a mixture-of-experts model that scores the experts for each token and picks the top few.

active-parameters.def: The parameters a model actually uses for one token. In a dense model it is all of them; in an MoE model it is the shared layers plus the chosen experts.

context-window.def: The maximum number of tokens, prompt and output together, a model can attend to in one request.

artificial-intelligence.def: Any technique that makes a computer do a task we would call intelligent if a person did it, such as planning, recognising or deciding. Hand-written rules count.

machine-learning.def: AI whose behaviour is learned from examples instead of written by hand.

deep-learning.def: Machine learning with neural networks of many layers, which learn their own intermediate features from data.

generative-ai.def: Models that create new content, such as text, images, audio or code, by learning what their training data looks like and producing new examples of it.

foundation-model.def: One large model pretrained on broad data and then adapted to many tasks, instead of one model trained per task.

agent.def: An LLM that works in a loop: it chooses a tool, looks at the result and decides the next step, until the task is done or a limit is reached.

language-model.def: A model that gives a probability to every possible next token, given the text so far. Generating text means picking a token, adding it and repeating.

llm.def: A transformer language model with billions of parameters, pretrained on a very large and broad text collection.

parameter.def: One learned number inside a model, also called a weight. An 8B model has about 8 billion of them.

embedding.def: A list of numbers (a vector) that stands for a token or a piece of text, so that similar meanings get similar numbers.

tokenizer.def: The part that splits text into tokens and turns them into id numbers. Each model family has its own, so the same text is a different number of tokens on different models.

training-inference.def: Training changes a model's parameters so its predictions improve; it is expensive and rare. Inference uses fixed parameters to answer; it is cheap per call and happens constantly.

hallucination.def: Fluent, confident output that is false, such as an invented citation, flag or policy clause.

training-cutoff.def: The date the training data ends. A model knows nothing after it unless the facts are put into its input.

grounding.def: Giving the model the source facts in its input and asking it to answer from them, with citations, so the answer can be checked.

vector.def: An ordered list of numbers, such as [0.2, -1.3, 0.7]. It can be pictured as an arrow; an embedding is a vector with hundreds or thousands of numbers.

cosine-similarity.def: How closely two vectors point the same way, from 1 (same direction) through 0 (unrelated) to -1 (opposite). It ignores their lengths, so it compares meaning rather than size.

base-rate.def: How common something is before any test, such as the share of transactions that are fraud. When it is low, most alarms from even a good detector are false.

confidence-interval.def: A range around a measured number that shows how far it could be off because only a sample was tested. More test cases make it narrower.

gradient.def: For each parameter, which way and how steeply the loss changes when that parameter grows a little.

gradient-descent.def: Training by many small steps: move every parameter a little in the direction that lowers the loss, then repeat.

learning-rate.def: How big each gradient-descent step is. Too small and training crawls; too big and it overshoots and can blow up.

loss-function.def: One number that says how wrong a model is on some examples. Training tries to make it smaller.

entropy.def: How unpredictable outcomes are, on average, measured in bits. A fair coin is 1 bit; a coin that always lands heads is 0.

kl-divergence.def: The extra surprise you pay for using a wrong guess of the probabilities instead of the true ones. Zero only when the guess is exactly right.

perplexity.def: A language model's loss turned into 'how many equally likely tokens it is choosing between'. Lower is better.

vectorisation.def: Writing a calculation as one operation on a whole array instead of a Python loop, so fast compiled code does the work.

reproducibility.def: Getting the same result again from the same inputs, which needs fixed seeds and recorded versions of code, data, models and prompts.

tensor.def: An array with any number of dimensions: a number, a vector, a matrix, or more, such as batch × tokens × features.

memory-bandwidth.def: How many bytes per second can be read from memory. Generating a token reads every weight once, so it often limits LLM speed more than raw compute does.

bf16.def: A 2-byte number format with the same range as 4-byte float32 but fewer digits of precision. The usual format for training and serving LLMs.

supervised-learning.def: Learning from examples that come with the right answer (a label), such as emails marked spam or not spam.

unsupervised-learning.def: Finding structure, such as groups or unusual items, in data that has no labels.

self-supervised-learning.def: Making labels from the data itself, such as hiding the next word and predicting it. It is how LLMs learn from trillions of tokens without human labelling.

reinforcement-learning.def: Learning by trying actions and getting rewards, so that actions that earned more reward become more likely.

baseline.def: The simplest sensible way to do a task, such as always giving the most common answer. A model is only worth what it adds over its baseline.

gradient-boosting.def: An ensemble that adds small decision trees one at a time, each fixing the errors of the ones before. Usually the strongest choice for tables of data.

k-means.def: A clustering method that repeats two steps: put each point with its nearest centre, then move each centre to the middle of its points.

class-imbalance.def: When one outcome is much rarer than the others, so a model can ignore it and still score high accuracy.

feature-engineering.def: Turning raw data into useful model inputs, such as a date into 'day of the week' or transactions into 'count in the last 24 hours'.

inter-annotator-agreement.def: How often two people labelling the same items agree, beyond what chance would give. Low agreement means the task itself is unclear.

overfitting.def: Learning the training examples so closely, noise included, that the model does worse on new data.

regularisation.def: Anything that stops a model fitting too closely, such as a penalty on large weights, limiting tree depth, dropout or stopping early.

data-leakage.def: Information in training data that would not be available when the model is really used, which makes test scores look better than real use will be.

train-validation-test.def: Three separate parts of the data: one to learn from, one to choose settings with, and one kept back to estimate real performance once.

precision-recall.def: Precision: of everything flagged, the share that was right. Recall: of everything that should have been flagged, the share that was caught.

f1.def: One number that combines precision and recall; it is high only when both are high.

calibration.def: Whether a model's scores mean what they say: of the cases scored 0.8, about 80% should really be positive.

error-analysis.def: Reading a sample of a model's mistakes, tagging each with a cause and counting the causes, so you fix the biggest one first.

hyperparameter.def: A setting chosen before training rather than learned, such as the learning rate or tree depth.

distribution-shift.def: When the data a model sees in use differs from the data it was trained on, such as new customers, new products or new kinds of fraud.

neuron.def: The basic unit of a neural network: multiply each input by a weight, add them up with a bias, and pass the result through an activation function.

activation-function.def: The bend applied after a neuron's weighted sum, such as ReLU or GELU. Without it, any number of layers acts like a single straight-line layer.

backpropagation.def: Working out every weight's gradient by applying the chain rule backwards from the loss through the layers, reusing the values saved on the way forward.

epoch.def: A batch is the group of examples used for one update, a step is one update, and an epoch is one full pass over the training data.

adamw.def: The default optimiser for transformers: it keeps a running average of each parameter's gradient and of its square, and gives every parameter its own step size. AdamW handles weight decay separately.

lr-schedule.def: Changing the learning rate during training; for LLMs, usually a short warm-up from near zero followed by a slow cosine decay.

gradient-accumulation.def: Adding up gradients over several small batches before one update, to act like a bigger batch than fits in memory.

vanishing-gradients.def: Gradients that shrink towards zero or grow without limit as they pass back through many layers, so early layers stop learning or training blows up.

normalisation.def: A layer that rescales activations to a steady size: BatchNorm across a batch, LayerNorm and RMSNorm within one example.

dropout.def: Switching off a random share of activations at each training step so the network cannot rely on any single path. It is turned off when the model is used.

gradient-clipping.def: Scaling the gradient down when its size passes a limit, often 1.0, to stop one bad batch causing a huge update.

representation-learning.def: A network learning useful internal vectors for its inputs as a side effect of its training task.

contrastive-learning.def: Training an encoder by pulling matching pairs (a question and its answer) together and pushing non-matching pairs apart. How text embedding models are trained.

cnn.def: A network that slides small learned filters across an image or sequence, finding the same local pattern wherever it appears.

rnn.def: A network that reads a sequence one step at a time and carries a hidden state forward. LSTMs and GRUs add gates so the state fades less.

autograd.def: A framework feature that records the operations you run and works out all the gradients for you when you call backward().

checkpoint.def: A saved copy of a model's weights, optimiser state and step number, so training can resume or the best version can be kept.

pretraining.def: The first and by far the most expensive training stage: next-token prediction on trillions of tokens of general text. It produces a base model.

base-model.def: A model straight out of pretraining. It continues text well but does not reliably follow instructions.

sft.def: Training a model on example conversations (instruction and good answer) so it learns to behave as an assistant or follow a format.

continued-pretraining.def: More next-token training on domain text, such as law, code or a new language, to shift what a model knows.

deduplication.def: Removing exact and near-duplicate documents from training data, usually with hashes and MinHash, so the model does not waste compute or memorise repeats.

contamination.def: Test or benchmark questions appearing in the training data, which makes scores on them meaningless.

data-mixture.def: The share of each source in training data, such as web, code, books and maths. It shapes what the model is good at.

scaling-laws.def: Measured rules for how loss falls as parameters, training tokens and compute grow; they let teams predict a big run from small ones.

mfu.def: The share of a GPU's peak arithmetic speed a training run really uses; 35–50% is typical for large runs.

chat-template.def: The exact text format, with special role tokens, that turns a list of chat messages into the token sequence a model was trained on.

loss-masking.def: Computing the training loss only on the tokens the model should learn to write, usually the assistant's replies, and ignoring the rest.

reward-model.def: A model trained on preference comparisons to give an answer a score for how good it is.

rlhf.def: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: generate answers, score them with a reward model and update the LLM to score higher, while a penalty keeps it close to the original.

dpo.def: Direct preference optimisation: training straight on pairs of preferred and rejected answers, with no separate reward model or RL loop.

rlvr.def: Reinforcement learning where the reward is checked automatically, such as unit tests passing or a maths answer matching. GRPO is a common algorithm for it.

reward-hacking.def: A model learning to score well on the reward without doing the task better, such as padding answers if longer ones score higher.

data-parallelism.def: Training with a full copy of the model on every GPU, each on different batches, averaging the gradients after every step.

zero-fsdp.def: Data parallelism that splits the optimiser state, gradients and even the weights across GPUs instead of copying them, so much bigger models fit.

tensor-parallelism.def: Splitting each big weight matrix across several GPUs so they share every layer's work. It needs very fast links between the GPUs.

pipeline-parallelism.def: Putting different layers on different GPUs and passing micro-batches through them like an assembly line; some GPUs wait at the start and end.

open-weights.def: A model whose trained weights you can download and run on your own hardware, as opposed to one you can only call through a provider's API.

few-shot.def: Putting a handful of worked input-and-output examples in the prompt so the model copies the format and decisions.

system-prompt.def: The developer's standing instructions sent with every request, separate from the user's message.

prompt-versioning.def: Storing prompts with an id and version, reviewing and testing every change, and logging the version with every request.

context-engineering.def: Deciding, for every model call, exactly what goes into the context window and in what order, within a token budget.

structured-output.def: Asking the model to answer as data in a declared format, usually JSON matching a schema, so code can read it.

constrained-decoding.def: Blocking any token that would break a schema or grammar while the model generates, so the output always has the right shape. It does not make the content true.

tool-calling.def: The model answering with a request to run a named function with arguments; your code checks it, runs it and sends back the result.

streaming.def: Sending the answer token by token as it is generated, so users see the first words sooner.

stateless-api.def: An API that remembers nothing between calls, so the application must send the whole conversation it wants the model to know every time.

compaction.def: Shrinking a long conversation's history by summarising old turns and extracting key facts, so it keeps fitting the context window.

exponential-backoff.def: Waiting longer after each failed attempt (1, 2, 4, 8 seconds), with a random part, so many clients do not retry at the same moment.

token-bucket.def: A rate limiter that refills a fixed number of allowances per second up to a maximum; requests wait until enough are available.

fallback.def: What happens when the main model keeps failing: a second model or provider, a cached answer or a polite message. It needs evaluating too.

deterministic-boundary.def: The line between what a model suggests and what code decides: the model interprets and proposes, rules in code check, decide and act.

acceptance-criteria.def: The measurable thresholds a feature must meet to ship, such as 92% correct overall and every critical case passing.

eval-set.def: A fixed, versioned collection of test cases with expected outcomes, sampled to look like real use and stratified so rare but important cases are included.

llm-judge.def: Using a model with a rubric to grade outputs. Cheap and scalable, but biased, so it must be checked against human labels first.

judge-bias.def: Systematic leanings of a model judge, such as preferring the first answer shown, longer answers or its own model family's style.

bootstrap.def: Estimating how much a score could move by re-drawing the test cases with replacement many times and looking at the spread of results.

groundedness.def: Whether every claim in an answer is supported by the sources it was given.

over-refusal.def: Declining to answer questions that could and should have been answered. Measured on a should-answer set, next to under-refusal on a should-refuse set.

oracle-context.def: Giving the model the known-correct documents directly, to measure answer quality separately from retrieval quality.

regression-suite.def: A fixed set of cases that passed before, run on every change and compared case by case, so a fix that breaks something else is visible.

adversarial-case.def: A test input built to make the system fail, such as a prompt injection, a jailbreak or a request for another customer's data.

ab-test.def: Randomly splitting real users between the current version and a new one and comparing outcomes, so a difference can be attributed to the change.

statistical-power.def: The chance an experiment detects a real effect of a given size. Small effects need many more users for the same power.

pass-at-k.def: pass@k: at least one of k runs succeeds. pass^k: all k runs succeed. Reliability in production depends on the second.

rag.def: Finding relevant passages in your own documents for each question and giving them to the model to answer from, with citations.

chunking.def: Splitting documents into passages small enough to embed, retrieve and fit into a prompt, ideally along sentence and section boundaries.

inverted-index.def: A map from each word to the documents that contain it, like the index at the back of a book, so keyword search never scans every document.

bm25.def: The standard keyword ranking: score documents by how often the query words appear, weighting rare words more and stopping repeated words from counting too much.

dense-retrieval.def: Search by meaning: embed the question and the passages as vectors and rank passages by similarity.

sparse-retrieval.def: A model that turns text into weighted keywords, including related words not in the text, stored in an ordinary inverted index.

ann.def: Finding the most similar vectors without comparing against all of them, trading a little recall for a lot of speed.

hnsw.def: A layered graph index for vectors: search hops between close neighbours on sparse upper layers, then refines on the full bottom layer.

vector-quantisation.def: Storing embedding vectors in fewer bits (int8, product quantisation or 1 bit per number) to save memory, often re-checking the top results with full vectors.

hybrid-retrieval.def: Running keyword and dense search together and merging their results, so both exact terms and paraphrases are found.

rrf.def: Merging ranked lists by adding up one divided by (a constant plus the rank) for each list. It uses ranks only, so the lists' scores never need matching.

reranker.def: A slower, more accurate model, usually a cross-encoder, that reads the question and each candidate passage together and re-orders the top results.

metadata-filtering.def: Restricting search results by fields such as tenant, language, date or permissions, ideally while searching rather than after.

query-rewriting.def: Turning a user's short or conversational question into better search queries, for example by adding context, expanding acronyms or splitting it into parts.

multi-hop.def: Answering in steps, where a fact found in one search is used to make the next search.

abstention.def: Saying the answer was not found instead of guessing, when retrieval finds nothing that supports an answer.

recall-at-k.def: Recall@k: the share of the relevant items that appear in the top k results. Precision@k: the share of the top k results that are relevant.

mrr.def: The average over queries of one divided by the position of the first relevant result: 1 if it is first, 0.5 if second.

ndcg.def: A ranking score that gives more credit for more relevant items and for putting them higher, scaled so a perfect ranking scores 1.

capacity-planning.def: Working out, from measured assumptions, how much storage, memory, compute and money a system will need at its target size and traffic.

message-queue.def: A durable buffer of work items between the stages of a pipeline, so each stage can scale, slow down or fail without losing work.

backpressure.def: Making a fast upstream stage slow down when a downstream stage cannot keep up, instead of letting work pile up until something runs out of memory.

dead-letter-queue.def: Where work items go after failing too many times, so they stop blocking the pipeline and someone can look at them.

idempotency.def: Doing the same operation twice has the same effect as doing it once, which makes retries and repeated deliveries safe.

ocr.def: Optical character recognition: turning images of text, such as scanned pages, into text.

incremental-indexing.def: Updating an index by processing only what changed (edits, additions and deletions) instead of rebuilding it.

lineage.def: The recorded history of every chunk: source, version, parser, chunker and embedding model, so you can explain an answer and rebuild exactly what a bug affected.

freshness.def: A measurable promise of how quickly changes in the source appear in the index, such as 99% of edits searchable within 10 minutes.

shard-replica.def: A shard is a slice of an index on one machine; a replica is a copy of a shard. Shards spread the data; replicas spread the reads and survive failures.

hot-tenant.def: One customer with far more data or traffic than the rest, overloading the machines it shares with others (a noisy neighbour).

acl-binding.def: Early binding stores who may see each chunk in the index and filters while searching; late binding checks the source system's permissions after retrieval.

tenant-isolation.def: Guaranteeing that one customer's queries can never retrieve another customer's data, enforced by the server rather than the prompt.

blue-green-index.def: Building a complete new index next to the live one, comparing them, switching traffic over and keeping the old one ready for rollback.

latency-percentile.def: The time within which 50%, 95% or 99% of requests finish. The higher percentiles show the slow tail that averages hide.

hierarchical-retrieval.def: Searching coarse summaries first (documents or sections), then only the passages inside the best matches.

late-interaction.def: Keeping one vector per token and matching each query token to its best document token, for finer matching than one vector per passage.

graphrag.def: Extracting entities and their relations into a knowledge graph and retrieving by following relations, for questions about connections and whole-corpus themes.

llm-workflow.def: A sequence of steps fixed in code, some of which call a model. Code, not the model, decides what happens next.

react.def: The basic agent loop: the model reasons, calls a tool, reads the result (the observation) and repeats until it answers or a limit stops it.

tool-schema.def: A tool’s name, a description written for the model and a strict JSON Schema for its arguments, checked in code before the tool runs.

agent-memory.def: What an agent keeps beyond the current context: records with an owner, a source and an expiry, recalled by relevance and recency.

durable-execution.def: Running a task so its progress survives crashes and restarts: each step is checkpointed and a resumed run continues instead of starting over.

idempotency-key.def: A unique key sent with a request that changes something; the server stores the result under it and returns that result for any retry with the same key.

saga.def: A multi-step process in which each step has a compensating action, so if a later step fails the earlier ones are undone in reverse order.

transactional-outbox.def: Writing a business change and the event announcing it in one database transaction, and letting a separate relay deliver the event, so the two never disagree.

human-in-the-loop.def: A person approving one exact proposed action, with its arguments and evidence, before it runs. Used for irreversible, financial or external actions.

mcp.def: An open protocol for connecting AI applications to tools, resources and prompts through servers, using JSON-RPC messages over stdio or HTTP.

tool-poisoning.def: Instructions hidden in a tool’s description or results that the model may follow, such as asking it to call another tool or send data elsewhere.

multi-agent.def: Several agents with their own instructions, tools and context that divide a task and pass results between them.

coordinator-worker.def: One agent splits a task, sends parts to worker agents with briefs, and combines what they return.

handoff.def: One agent passing the conversation to another, with a structured summary of what is known, so the user sees one continuous conversation.

task-brief.def: What a worker agent receives: objective, scope, allowed tools, budget, deadline and the shape of the result to return.

message-contract.def: A typed, versioned schema for the requests and results agents exchange, checked by both sides like an API contract.

a2a.def: An open protocol for agents from different frameworks or companies to discover each other and exchange tasks and results.

task-dag.def: Tasks with dependencies and no cycles, so each task starts only when the tasks it needs have finished.

error-compounding.def: Small error rates multiplying along a chain of steps: ten steps that are each 95% right are all right only about 60% of the time.

confused-deputy.def: A program with broad permissions tricked into using them for someone who should not have them.

token-exchange.def: Trading an incoming access token for a new one that is valid only at the next service and carries the same or fewer permissions.

ablation.def: Removing one component and measuring again, to find out whether it really contributes.

distillation.def: Training a small “student” model on the checked outputs of a large “teacher” model, so the task runs cheaper and faster.

labelling-guideline.def: The versioned written rules annotators follow: task definition, output format, decision rules, worked examples and what to do when unsure.

peft.def: Fine-tuning that freezes the base model and trains a small number of new parameters, such as LoRA adapters.

lora.def: Low-rank adaptation: next to a frozen weight matrix, train two thin matrices whose product is a small correction, then keep it as an adapter or merge it in.

qlora.def: LoRA on a base model stored in 4 bits, which cuts memory enough to fine-tune large models on one GPU.

field-fabrication.def: An extractor filling a field that the document does not contain, usually because training rarely showed the field absent.

hard-negative.def: A passage that looks relevant to a query but is not, used in training to teach a retriever fine distinctions.

catastrophic-forgetting.def: A fine-tuned model losing general abilities it had before, such as other languages or safe refusals.

canary.def: A unique made-up string planted in training data; if the model can complete it later, it has memorised training records.

model-card.def: A model’s release document: intended use, training data, evaluation results, limitations and licence.

model-registry.def: A store of immutable model versions linked to the run, data and code that produced them, with stages such as staging and production.

ttft.def: How long a user waits before the first word of the answer appears: queueing plus prefill of the whole prompt.

itl.def: The time between streamed output tokens, set by how long one decode step takes. Also called time per output token.

continuous-batching.def: Re-forming the batch at every decode step, so finished sequences leave at once and waiting requests take their slots.

paged-attention.def: Storing the KV cache in small fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, like memory pages, so little memory is reserved but unused.

prefix-caching.def: Keeping the KV cache of a prompt’s shared beginning, such as a system prompt, and reusing it so later requests skip that part of prefill.

weight-quantisation.def: Storing a model’s weights in fewer bits, such as 8 or 4, to save memory and speed up decoding, at some cost in quality.

speculative-decoding.def: A small draft model proposes several tokens and the large model checks them in one pass, keeping the ones it agrees with; the output is unchanged.

disaggregated-serving.def: Running prefill and decode on separate GPU pools and passing the KV cache between them, so each pool is sized for its own bottleneck.

cold-start.def: The minutes a new replica needs before serving: getting a GPU node, pulling the image, loading weights and warming up.

admission-control.def: Limiting how much work a server accepts, with a cap on concurrent sequences and a bounded queue, so accepted requests still meet their targets.

break-even-volume.def: The monthly usage at which self-hosting a model costs the same as paying per token for an API.

littles-law.def: In a stable system, the average number of requests in flight equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends inside.

slo.def: A target for a measured indicator over a window, such as 99.5% of requests answered within 10 seconds over 28 days.

error-budget.def: The failure an SLO allows: with a 99.9% target, 0.1% of requests may fail. Spending it fast triggers alerts and slows risky releases.

workload-separation.def: Giving ingestion, retrieval, generation and agent work their own capacity, so a bulk job cannot starve interactive users.

semantic-cache.def: Reusing a stored answer for a new request that is similar, not identical. Risky: similar questions can need different answers.

model-gateway.def: One service between applications and all model backends that handles routing, credentials, quotas, fallbacks, metering and logging.

fair-queuing.def: Sharing scarce capacity between tenants in proportion to their share, instead of first come first served, so one tenant’s burst stays its own problem.

load-shedding.def: Rejecting some requests early and cheaply when overloaded, lowest priority first, so the rest still meet their deadlines.

circuit-breaker.def: A wrapper that stops calling a failing dependency for a while after too many errors, failing fast or using a fallback, then tries a few calls before resuming.

graceful-degradation.def: A planned ladder of reduced service levels, such as a smaller model or cached answers only, used instead of failing outright.

rpo-rto.def: Recovery point objective: how much recent data you may lose. Recovery time objective: how quickly service must return.

coordinated-omission.def: A load-test error where the tester waits for slow replies before sending more, so it never records the requests that would have queued.

cost-per-success.def: Everything a feature costs, including retries and people handling failures, divided by the tasks that really succeeded.

projected-capacity.def: Capacity worked out from measured figures and assumptions, as opposed to performance measured directly or usage seen in production.

threat-modelling.def: Walking each component and data flow to ask what can go wrong, who could cause it, and which controls prevent, detect or limit it.

lethal-trifecta.def: An assistant that has private data, reads untrusted content and has a way to send data out. Together they make injection-driven leaks possible; remove one.

prompt-injection.def: Instructions in user input or in content the model reads (a page, an email, a tool result) that try to override what the system told it to do.

least-privilege.def: Giving each user, service, agent and tool only the permissions its job needs, for as short a time as possible.

sandboxing.def: Running code or browsing in an isolated environment with no internal network access, limited resources and a fresh start for each task.

data-minimisation.def: Sending a model only the data a task needs, with personal details removed or replaced by placeholders where possible.

audit-log.def: An append-only record of who accessed what, what the model was given, what it did and on whose behalf, kept for investigations and regulators.

ai-bom.def: A software bill of materials extended with the models, datasets and versions a system uses.

model-supply-chain.def: Everything between a model’s publisher and your production: hubs, files, custom code and dependencies, any of which can be tampered with.

red-teaming.def: Deliberately attacking your own system before others do, with automated scanners and human creativity, and turning findings into regression tests.

guardrail.def: A check around a model, such as an input or output classifier or a rule, that blocks or flags content against a policy. Its catch and false-positive rates must be measured.

ai-regulation.def: Laws and standards that apply to AI systems, such as the EU AI Act, GDPR, the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001, which engineers translate into controls and evidence.

distributed-trace.def: The path of one request through a system as a tree of timed spans, linked by a trace id that travels across services, queues and agents.

correlation-id.def: An id attached to every log, span, row and ticket about one request or task, so all of it can be found together. Usually the trace id.

opentelemetry.def: The vendor-neutral standard, SDKs and Collector for producing, processing and exporting traces, metrics and logs.

critical-path.def: The chain of dependent steps that decides a request’s total time; making any step off it faster changes nothing.

golden-signals.def: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation: the four operational measurements every service should have.

implicit-feedback.def: Quality signals inferred from what users do rather than say, such as rephrasing the question, copying the answer or opening a ticket.

cost-attribution.def: Tagging every model call with tenant, feature, user and prompt version, so spend can be grouped and explained.

tail-sampling.def: Deciding which traces to keep after they finish: all errors, slow and flagged ones, plus a small random share of the rest.

quality-drift.def: Answer quality slowly declining as users, products, documents or models change, without any single failure.

burn-rate-alert.def: An alert on how fast the error budget is being used, checked over a short and a long window, rather than on every error.

runbook.def: The written steps for one alert: what it means, how to confirm it, first mitigations, who to call and how to check recovery.

eval-flywheel.def: The routine of turning production failures into evaluation cases, fixing the cause, and gating releases on the growing suite.

semantic-conventions.def: Agreed names and meanings for telemetry attributes, such as OpenTelemetry’s gen_ai.* names for model calls, so tools understand each other’s data.

release-manifest.def: One record of every version that makes up the deployed system: code, prompts, models, index, configuration and evaluation suite, under one release id.

infrastructure-as-code.def: Defining servers, GPU pools, databases, permissions and alerts in reviewed code that pipelines apply, instead of clicking in consoles.

environment-promotion.def: Moving the same built artefact from development to staging to production, with only configuration changing between them.

release-gate.def: An automated check that blocks a change from moving forward when a quality, safety, performance or cost threshold is not met.

shadow-deployment.def: Sending a copy of real traffic to a new version and comparing its outputs, while users still see the old version’s answers.

canary-release.def: Giving a new version a small share of real traffic, comparing it with the current version, and widening or rolling back automatically.

model-upgrade.def: Moving a feature to a new model version, treated as a release: compatibility checks, prompt re-tuning, shadow, canary and a rollback window.

retraining-trigger.def: A defined condition, such as an SLO breach, measured drift or enough new labelled data, that opens work to re-tune or retrain.

operational-readiness.def: A check before launch or handover that a system can be run: SLOs, alerts, tested runbooks, on-call, capacity, recovery, security and budgets.

pass-condition.def: The measurable result, agreed before building, that decides whether a milestone is done, such as a paired gain whose interval excludes zero.

evidence-category.def: Whether a number was simulated, measured locally, projected from measurements, or seen operating in production. Every claim should carry one.
